section.title: The Binding of Isaac
section.sectionRationale: This is the climb of Abraham's faith, the fiercest test in Genesis. God asks for the son of promise, Abraham obeys, and at the last moment God Himself provides a substitute. The scene reaches forward, on the same mountain range, to another Father and another Son.
section.thesis: God tests Abraham to the very edge, and Abraham trusts that God will provide; the ram caught in the thicket dies in Isaac's place, and God renews His oath to bless the whole world through the seed of the obedient son.
section.frameNote: Five scenes: the command; the journey of obedience; the binding and the stayed hand; the oath renewed; and the family of Nahor, which quietly introduces Rebekah.

units.label: The command to sacrifice
units.note: take your son, your only son

verses.text: Some time later God {{tested|tested}} Abraham and said to him, “Abraham!” “Here I am,” he answered.
“Take your son,” God said, “your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains, which I will show you.”

So Abraham got up early the next morning, saddled his donkey, and took along two of his servants and his son Isaac. He split the wood for a {{burntoffering|burnt offering}} and set out for the place God had designated.
On the third day Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance.
“Stay here with the donkey,” Abraham told his servants. “The boy and I will go over there to worship, and then we will return to you.”
Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it on his son Isaac. He himself carried the fire and the sacrificial knife, and the two of them walked on together.
Then Isaac said to his father Abraham, “My father!” “Here I am, my son,” he replied. “The fire and the wood are here,” said Isaac, “but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?”
Abraham answered, “God Himself will {{provide|provide}} the lamb for the burnt offering, my son.” And the two walked on together.

units.label: The binding and the stayed hand
units.note: the ram in place of his son

verses.text: When they arrived at the place God had designated, Abraham built the altar there and arranged the wood. He bound his son Isaac and placed him on the altar, atop the wood.
Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.
Just then the angel of the LORD called out to him from heaven, “Abraham, Abraham!” “Here I am,” he replied.
“Do not lay a hand on the boy or do anything to him,” said the angel, “for now I know that you {{fear|fear}} God, since you have not withheld your only son from me.”
Then Abraham looked up and saw behind him a ram in a thicket, caught by its horns. So he went and took the ram and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son.
And Abraham called that place The LORD Will Provide. So to this day it is said, “On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided.”

units.label: The oath renewed
units.note: in your seed all nations blessed

verses.text: And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham from heaven a second time,
saying, “By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, that because you have done this and have not withheld your only son,
I will surely bless you, and I will multiply your descendants like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore. Your descendants will possess the gates of their enemies.
And through your offspring all nations of the earth will be blessed, because you have obeyed My voice.”
Abraham went back to his servants, and they got up and set out together for Beersheba. And Abraham settled in Beersheba.
Some time later, Abraham was told, “Milcah has also borne sons to your brother Nahor:
Uz the firstborn, his brother Buz, Kemuel (the father of Aram),
Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel.”
And Bethuel became the father of Rebekah. Milcah bore these eight sons to Abraham’s brother Nahor.
Moreover, Nahor’s concubine, whose name was Reumah, bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.

tested.gloss: To test, try, or prove. A test in Scripture is not God gathering information He lacks, but a trial that reveals and refines what is truly in a person's heart. God tests Abraham to bring his faith to full expression, not to trip him up, and the test proves his trust real.

burntoffering.gloss: A whole burnt offering, from a root meaning to go up, as the smoke ascends to God. Unlike other sacrifices, the whole animal is consumed, a total gift given wholly to God. The word frames the entire ordeal: Isaac is asked as an olah, and a ram is finally given up in his place.

provide.gloss: To see, and by extension to see to, to provide. Abraham says God will see to the lamb, and names the place The LORD Will See, or Provide. Divine provision here is God seeing the need in advance and supplying it Himself, the same word behind the saying, on the mountain of the LORD it will be provided.

fear.gloss: To fear, reverence, or stand in awe. The fear of God is not cringing terror but a reverent trust that holds nothing back from Him. The angel says Abraham has shown this fear by not withholding his son, proving a heart that treasures God above even the dearest gift.

basic.context: After years of waiting, God gave Abraham the promised son, Isaac. Now God tells him to offer that very son as a sacrifice. Abraham obeys, step by agonising step, until God stops his hand and provides a ram instead. The key question is whether Abraham will trust and fear God even when God seems to ask for the promise back.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real event, told to reveal Abraham's tested faith and God's provision, not a command for anyone to imitate. God never intended Isaac to die, and He forbids human sacrifice elsewhere. The question the chapter presses is what genuine, God fearing trust looks like when everything is on the line.
basic.originalLanguages: God tests, nasah, Abraham, to prove and refine his faith. Isaac is asked as an olah, a whole burnt offering given entirely to God. Abraham says God will provide, raah, literally see to, the lamb, and names the mountain The LORD Will Provide. The angel says Abraham fears, yare, God, a reverent trust that holds nothing back.
basic.typology: The parallels to Christ are striking: a beloved, only son, carrying the wood up a mountain in the region later called Moriah, a father who does not spare his son, and a substitute who dies in the son's place. The ram caught in the thicket foreshadows the Lamb God would provide at the cross.
basic.christ: Where Abraham's hand was stayed, God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all. Isaac carried the wood; Jesus carried His cross. The saying on the mountain of the LORD it will be provided finds its answer at Calvary, near Moriah, where God provides the true Lamb.
basic.god: God is the tester who refines faith, and the provider who supplies what He demands. He never wanted Isaac dead; He wanted Abraham's whole heart, and then He Himself gave the substitute. He is faithful to His oath, swearing by Himself to bless the world.
basic.crossReferences: John 3:16 speaks of God giving His only Son. Romans 8:32 says God did not spare His own Son. Hebrews 11 says Abraham reckoned God able to raise the dead. James 2 points to Abraham's faith proven by works.
basic.oneStory: The promise nearly dies on the altar, then God provides a substitute and renews His oath to bless all nations through Abraham's seed. That seed is Christ, and the mountain of provision points straight to the cross where the true Lamb is given.

context.literary:
The narrator tells the reader at once what Abraham does not know: 'God tested Abraham,' verse 1. We watch the whole journey knowing it is a test, while Abraham walks it as a command. That gap is the source of the chapter's tension.

The story is built around three calls and three answers of 'Here I am.' God calls, verse 1; Isaac calls, 'My father!' verse 7; the angel calls, 'Abraham, Abraham!' verse 11. Each time Abraham answers with the same word, hinneni. He is fully present to God, fully present to his son, and fully present to God again at the moment of crisis. The three answers mark the three turning points of the story.

The telling is famously spare. Abraham's feelings are never described. There is no conversation on the three day journey except one exchange, verses 7 and 8, framed by the refrain 'the two of them walked on together,' verses 6 and 8. Isaac speaks in only one exchange in the whole chapter, and what he says is a single question about the lamb. The narrator slows down dramatically at the altar, verses 9 and 10, listing every action: built, arranged, bound, placed, reached out, took. Then the angel's voice breaks in.

The chapter deliberately recalls Abraham's first call. 'Go' in verse 2 is the same Hebrew phrase as 'go' in Genesis 12:1, and both commands narrow step by step: 'your country, your kindred, and your father's household' there, 'your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love' here. The life of faith that began with giving up the past ends with offering up the future.

The chapter is framed by two notes of 'Some time later,' verses 1 and 20. The second introduces the family of Nahor, twelve sons in all, eight by Milcah and four by Reumah, matching the twelve sons of Ishmael, Genesis 25:13-16, and anticipating the twelve sons of Jacob. Among these names comes Rebekah, verse 23. Having just been promised descendants like the stars, Abraham hears of the woman through whom the promise will continue.
context.historical:
God sends Abraham to 'the land of Moriah,' verse 2, and the journey from Beersheba takes until the third day, verse 4. The only other time Scripture uses the name is 2 Chronicles 3:1, where Solomon builds the temple 'on Mount Moriah' in Jerusalem, on the threshing floor David had bought. The Chronicler thus ties Abraham's altar to the place of Israel's sacrifices, and a journey of about three days from Beersheba to the Jerusalem hills is realistic.

The details are those of a real burnt offering. Abraham splits the wood before he leaves, verse 3, since suitable wood might be scarce on the mountain. He carries the fire, probably coals in a container, and the knife, verse 6. Isaac is old enough to carry the wood for a whole burnt offering, verse 6, so he is at least a youth, probably stronger than his aged father, which suggests he allowed himself to be bound.

The command would not have sounded unimaginable in Abraham's world, and that is part of its horror. Child sacrifice was practised among some of Israel's neighbours. The king of Moab offered his firstborn son as a burnt offering on his city wall, 2 Kings 3:27. Israel's law condemned it absolutely: 'You must not give any of your children to be sacrificed to Molech,' Leviticus 18:21, and the nations 'even burn their sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to their gods,' Deuteronomy 12:31. Through Jeremiah God says of such sacrifices, 'something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind,' Jeremiah 7:31.

Yet Israel's law also said that every firstborn son belonged to the LORD and had to be redeemed, Exodus 13:13 and 34:20. The first hearers would have understood Genesis 22 both as a decisive rejection of child sacrifice, since God stops the knife, and as a picture of the principle that the firstborn is God's and is spared only by a substitute.

In Jewish tradition this chapter is called the Akedah, the binding, from the verb in verse 9, and it is read at the New Year.
context.canonical:
The chapter becomes a touchstone for faith and obedience across both Testaments. The oath of verses 16 to 18 is confirmed to Isaac, 'because Abraham listened to My voice,' Genesis 26:3-5. Moses appeals to it when Israel has sinned with the golden calf: 'Remember Your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, to whom You swore by Your very self,' Exodus 32:13. The oath God swore on Moriah becomes the ground of Israel's intercession.

The prophets reject any thought that God wants human sacrifice. Micah asks, 'Shall I present my firstborn for my transgression?' and answers that the LORD requires justice, mercy and humility, Micah 6:7-8. Genesis 22 had already given that answer at the altar.

The New Testament uses the chapter in several directions. Hebrews 11:17-19 presents it as the height of Abraham's faith: he 'reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.' James 2:21-23 presents it as the proof that Abraham's faith was real: 'his faith was perfected by what he did,' fulfilling the word that 'Abraham believed God' from Genesis 15:6. Hebrews 6:13-18 builds its whole argument for Christian assurance on the oath of Genesis 22:16-17, 'since He had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself.' Peter quotes verse 18 in Acts 3:25, and Paul reads the promised 'offspring' as Christ, Galatians 3:16.

Most striking are the echoes in the language of the gospel. Paul writes that God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32, and the Greek verb 'spare' is the one the Septuagint uses in Genesis 22:12 and 22:16 for Abraham not withholding Isaac. The voice at Jesus' baptism calls Him 'My beloved Son,' Mark 1:11, echoing the Septuagint's rendering of 'your only son' in verse 2. John speaks of God giving 'His one and only Son,' John 3:16, and points to Jesus as 'the Lamb of God,' John 1:29, the answer to Isaac's question.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to understand what it means to fear God. The angel's verdict, 'now I know that you fear God,' verse 12, is the point of the story. Fear of God here is not terror but a trust that holds nothing back, a faith that will obey even when obedience seems to destroy the very promise God gave. Israel was to learn that the gifts of God must never replace the Giver.

He also wanted them to know that the LORD is not like the gods of Canaan. He does not want the blood of children. He tests, He provides, and He takes the life of a substitute in place of the son. Every firstborn Israelite who was redeemed, every lamb offered on the altar in Jerusalem, carried the memory of this mountain: 'On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided,' verse 14.

Finally, he wanted Israel to see the foundation of their existence. The promise of countless descendants and blessing for all nations was confirmed here by God's own oath, verses 16 to 18. Israel existed because God had sworn by Himself to a man who did not withhold his son. When Israel failed, as at Sinai, they could appeal to that oath, and God would keep it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a unique test given to one man at a unique moment in redemptive history. It does not prescribe that anyone offer a child to God, and God's own intervention, together with the later law and the prophets, rules that out entirely, Leviticus 18:21 and Jeremiah 7:31. Anyone who claims a divine command to harm another person is contradicted by this very chapter, where God stops the knife.

What does carry over is the shape of faith. Believers are tested, though not in this way: 'the proven character of your faith,' Peter writes, is 'more precious than gold,' 1 Peter 1:7. God's testing is not temptation, since 'God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone,' James 1:13; He tests to reveal and strengthen faith, never to make it fail. Christians are called to hold God's gifts, even the best of them, with open hands, and to trust that God will provide what He requires. Abraham's words 'God Himself will provide' become a confession every believer can make.

debates.question: In what sense does God test Abraham, and what does 'now I know' mean?

views.label: The test reveals and proves
views.case: God's knowledge is not in question. Deuteronomy 8:2 uses the same language of testing Israel 'in order to know what was in your heart,' meaning to bring it into the open. 'Now I know' means that Abraham's fear of God has been demonstrated in action, before God, Abraham, and every later reader.

views.label: The test forms and matures
views.case: The trial is not only demonstration but formation. Exodus 20:20 says God comes to test His people 'so that the fear of Him may be before you.' Testing produces the fear of God that it reveals. Abraham comes down the mountain a man who has learned for himself that the LORD provides.

debates.bearing: Both views hold together. The test is for Abraham's good and God's glory, not a probe by an ignorant God, and it ends not in death but in provision and renewed promise.

debates.question: How can God command Abraham to sacrifice his son?

views.label: God's right as Giver of life
views.case: Isaac was God's gift, born by miracle, and God has the right to ask for what He gave. Some, most famously the philosopher Kierkegaard, have stressed that Abraham's faith meant obeying God even where it seemed to overturn ordinary ethics. On this view the command stands as a real demand, relieved only by God's intervention.

views.label: A test never meant to be completed
views.case: The narrator tells us from the start that this is a test, verse 1. God never intended Isaac to die, and the story ends by forbidding the act. Abraham's words 'we will return' and 'God Himself will provide,' verses 5 and 8, suggest he expected God to act, and Hebrews 11:19 says he reckoned God could raise the dead.

views.label: A lesson against child sacrifice
views.case: Others stress that in a world where gods demanded children, the story shows the LORD stopping the knife and supplying a ram. The chapter's lasting effect in Israel was to establish that God does not want human sacrifice, a point the law and prophets make explicit.

debates.bearing: The second and third views are both supported by the text, and the first rightly insists that God's claim on Isaac was real. The chapter resolves the tension not by softening the demand but by God's provision of a substitute, a resolution that points ahead to the one Son God did not spare.

debates.question: What did Abraham mean when he told his servants 'we will return to you' in verse 5?

views.label: A confession of faith
views.case: The verbs are plural: we will worship, we will return. Hebrews 11:19 interprets this as Abraham's conviction that God could raise Isaac from the dead, since God had said 'through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned,' Genesis 21:12. Abraham could not see how, but he believed both the command and the promise.

views.label: A protective word to the servants
views.case: Some suggest Abraham was shielding the servants, and perhaps Isaac, from the truth, so that they would not interfere. His reply to Isaac in verse 8 would then be a way of avoiding the question.

debates.bearing: The New Testament settles the matter in favour of faith. Hebrews reads Abraham's words as genuine trust, and the story bears it out: God did provide, and both did return. Abraham's words turned out to be more true than he could have known.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond testing, burnt offering, providing and fear, several words and constructions carry the chapter.

The answer 'Here I am,' hinneni, verses 1, 7 and 11, is more than a reply to a name. It is a statement of readiness and availability. Moses answers God with it at the bush, Exodus 3:4, and Isaiah uses the same word in the temple, 'Here am I. Send me!' Isaiah 6:8. Abraham gives the same answer to God and to his son; he is equally available to both, which is what makes the test so agonising.

The command 'Go' in verse 2 is the phrase lekh lekha, the same words as Genesis 12:1. The repetition ties the first and last great tests of Abraham's life together.

'Your only son,' verses 2, 12 and 16, is yachid, one, only, unique. Abraham had another son, Ishmael, but Isaac was the only son of promise, and after chapter 21 the only son at home. The word appears for Jephthah's daughter, 'his only child,' Judges 11:34, and for the deepest mourning Israel knew, 'as one mourns for an only child,' Zechariah 12:10 and Amos 8:10. The Septuagint renders yachid in all three verses of Genesis 22 with agapetos, beloved. That rendering stands behind the voice from heaven, 'You are My beloved Son,' Mark 1:11. Hebrews 11:17 chooses the other sense, 'one and only son.'

'Whom you love,' verse 2, is the first time the Bible uses the word love, ahav. It is spoken first of a father's love for his son, in the very sentence asking him to give that son up.

Isaac asks, 'where is the lamb,' verse 7, using seh, a lamb or kid of the flock. It is the word used for the Passover lamb, Exodus 12:3, and for the Servant who was 'led like a lamb to the slaughter,' Isaiah 53:7. Abraham's answer in verse 8 is literally 'God will see for Himself the lamb.' The verb ra'ah, to see, is used in the sense of to see to or provide, and the words 'for Himself' stress that God is the one who will supply His own offering.

In verse 9 Abraham 'bound' Isaac. The verb aqad occurs only here in the Old Testament, which is why the chapter came to be called the Akedah, the binding. It is the ordinary word for tying an animal's legs, and it underlines that Isaac is treated as the sacrifice.

The ram is offered 'in place of his son,' verse 13. The preposition tachat means under, instead of, in place of. It is the language of substitution.

The name in verse 14 is YHWH Yireh, as the BSB footnote notes, 'the LORD will see' or 'provide.' The proverb that follows uses a passive form of the same verb, which can be read either 'it will be provided' or 'He will be seen.' On the mountain of the LORD, God both provides and appears. Many also hear an echo of the verb in the name Moriah itself.

Finally, the oath of verses 16 and 17 uses the doubled construction twice, 'blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply,' which the BSB renders 'I will surely bless... and I will multiply.' Hebrews 6:14 quotes it. God's emphatic speech matches the emphatic obedience He has seen.

typology.type: The only, beloved son offered by his father
typology.fulfillment: Abraham was asked to give 'your only son Isaac, whom you love.' The New Testament uses the same language of the Father and the Son: 'My beloved Son,' Mark 1:11, and 'He gave His one and only Son,' John 3:16. Paul's 'He who did not spare His own Son,' Romans 8:32, uses the Septuagint's verb from Genesis 22:16. The escalation is decisive. Abraham's hand was stopped and his son was spared; the Father's hand was not stopped. Isaac was a son given by God and returned to Him; Christ is the eternal Son who came willingly: 'I lay it down of My own accord,' John 10:18.

typology.type: Isaac carrying the wood up the mountain
typology.fulfillment: Abraham 'placed it on his son Isaac,' verse 6, and the son carried the wood of his own sacrifice uphill. John records that Jesus went out 'carrying His own cross' to Golgotha, John 19:17. The correspondence is visual and striking, and the difference is great. Isaac carried wood without knowing what it was for and came down again alive. Jesus carried the wood knowing He would die on it, and 'for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame,' Hebrews 12:2. The type prepares us for the cross; it cannot bear what the cross bore.

typology.type: The ram offered in place of the son
typology.fulfillment: The ram dies 'in place of his son,' verse 13, and Isaac lives. Here for the first time Scripture says in so many words that a sacrifice dies in place of someone, and the whole sacrificial system grows from that idea. John the Baptist points to the fulfilment: 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!' John 1:29. Peter speaks of 'the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' who 'was known before the foundation of the world,' 1 Peter 1:19-20. The type falls short, as Hebrews says: 'it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins,' Hebrews 10:4. The ram saved one boy from one altar; Christ bears the sin of the world.

typology.type: The mountain of the LORD where He provides
typology.fulfillment: Abraham named the place 'The LORD Will Provide,' and a proverb grew: 'On the mountain of the LORD it will be provided.' The Chronicler locates Solomon's temple on Mount Moriah, 2 Chronicles 3:1, so that all Israel's sacrifices were offered on or near this mountain. Jesus was crucified in the same city, just 'outside the city gate,' Hebrews 13:12, and there God provided the sacrifice the temple could only foreshadow. The escalation is that the temple itself is replaced: in the new creation 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22.

typology.type: Isaac received back as from death on the third day
typology.fulfillment: From the moment of the command Isaac was, in Abraham's mind, as good as dead, and on the third day, verse 4, they reached the place where he was given back. Hebrews says Abraham 'reasoned that God could raise the dead, and in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death,' Hebrews 11:19. The echo of Christ's resurrection 'on the third day,' 1 Corinthians 15:4, is suggestive rather than explicit, and should be held lightly. But Hebrews makes the essential link. Isaac's return was a figure; Christ actually died and actually rose, and in Him all who believe will be raised.

study.christ:
No Old Testament narrative runs closer to the cross than this one, and the New Testament writers knew it. The chapter points to Christ in at least four ways.

First, by the father and the son. The command, 'Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love,' piles up words to make Abraham feel the weight of what is asked. The New Testament uses the same terms of God's own Son. At the baptism and again at the transfiguration the Father calls Jesus 'My beloved Son,' and in the parable of the tenants the owner has 'one beloved son' whom he finally sends, Mark 12:6. The heart of the gospel is that God did what He did not require of Abraham: 'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. Where the angel said 'Do not lay a hand on the boy,' there was no voice from heaven to stop the cross.

Second, by the substitute. Isaac's question, 'where is the lamb?' is the question of the Old Testament. Every lamb offered in the temple answered it partially and temporarily. John the Baptist answers it fully: 'Look, the Lamb of God,' John 1:29. Abraham's words, 'God Himself will provide the lamb,' turn out to mean more than he knew. God did not merely supply a lamb; He gave Himself in His Son. 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21.

Third, by the willing son. Isaac, strong enough to carry the wood, lets his aged father bind him. Nothing in the text suggests he resisted. Jesus goes further still, praying in another garden near Jerusalem, 'Not as I will, but as You will,' Matthew 26:39, and becoming 'obedient to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:8. Isaiah says 'it was the LORD's will to crush Him,' Isaiah 53:10, and yet the Son laid down His life of His own accord, John 10:18. The Father and the Son walked to the cross together, as Abraham and Isaac 'walked on together.'

Fourth, by the oath and the offspring. The chapter ends with God swearing by Himself that through Abraham's offspring all nations will be blessed, verse 18. Peter tells the crowd in Jerusalem that this promise is fulfilled when God raised up His Servant and sent Him 'to bless you,' Acts 3:25-26. Paul says the offspring is one person, Christ, Galatians 3:16. The blessing sworn on Moriah reaches the nations through the Son who was not spared.

Jesus Himself said, 'Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad,' John 8:56. Whatever Abraham saw on Moriah, the chapter lets every later reader see more.

A caution guards the reading. Isaac is a type, not a double of Christ. He did not die, he did not atone, and he did not know what was happening until the binding. The typology works because the New Testament draws these lines itself, and because the contrasts are as important as the likenesses. Abraham's love was tested; God's love was shown. Abraham gave back a son he had received; God gave the Son who is Himself God.
study.god:
This chapter reveals God as the one who tests. That is uncomfortable, but it is plainly stated in verse 1. The Bible distinguishes testing from temptation. Temptation aims at failure; God 'does not tempt anyone,' James 1:13. Testing aims at proving and strengthening. Exodus 20:20 puts it plainly: God comes to test His people 'so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning.' God tested Abraham not because He was unsure of him, but so that Abraham's faith might be revealed, completed and rewarded.

He is also the God who provides. The name YHWH Yireh, 'the LORD will see,' combines His knowledge and His provision. He sees the need before we reach it; the ram was already caught in the thicket before Abraham looked up. The church father Augustine prayed, 'Give what you command, and command what you will,' and this chapter is the great illustration of that prayer. God demands the offering and then supplies it Himself.

He is the God who claims first place. Isaac was God's own gift, the fulfilment of God's promise, and yet God asked for him. The point was not that the gift was bad but that the gift must never become a rival to the Giver. The command 'whom you love' is the Bible's first word about love, and it concerns a love that must be surrendered to God before it can be safely kept.

He is the God who does not want human sacrifice. The same God who tested Abraham stopped the knife, and later declared that burning children was 'something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind,' Jeremiah 7:31. The chapter does not make God like the gods of Canaan; it separates Him from them forever.

He is the God who binds Himself by oath. 'By Myself I have sworn,' verse 16. Since there is no one greater, God swears by His own name, and Hebrews says this was done 'to make the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise,' Hebrews 6:17. God's promise and God's oath are 'two unchangeable things,' Hebrews 6:18, and the Christian's hope rests on them.

The chapter also shows the mystery of the angel of the LORD. The angel speaks from heaven, yet says 'you have not withheld your only son from Me,' verse 12, and 'By Myself I have sworn, declares the LORD,' verse 16. The messenger speaks as God Himself. Many Christian interpreters have seen here a hint of the Son before His incarnation, though the text does not say so directly.

The chapter holds together demand and provision, severity and grace, in one God. For worship it teaches us to hold every gift with open hands, to trust God's provision when we cannot see it, and to marvel that the God who spared Abraham's son did not spare His own.

crossReferences.note: Abraham's first call uses the same command, 'Go,' and the same narrowing sequence, 'your country, your kindred, and your father's household.' Genesis 22 is the bookend of that call: he began by giving up his past and ends by offering up his future, and in both God promises blessing for all the families of the earth.

Hebrews says Abraham 'reasoned that God could raise the dead' and 'in a sense, he did receive Isaac back from death.' It explains how Abraham could hold together God's command to sacrifice Isaac and God's promise that 'through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned.'

James says Abraham was 'justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac,' and that his faith 'was perfected by what he did.' The obedience of Genesis 22 proves and completes the faith first credited to Abraham as righteousness in Genesis 15:6.

'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.' Paul's verb for 'spare' echoes the Greek of Genesis 22:12 and 22:16. The Father's love goes further than Abraham's: God stopped Abraham's hand but did not stop His own.

God 'gave His one and only Son' out of love for the world. The phrase recalls Genesis 22:2, 'your only son... whom you love.' What God asked of Abraham and then withheld, He Himself carried out in giving His Son.

John the Baptist sees Jesus and says, 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!' This answers Isaac's question in Genesis 22:7, 'where is the lamb?' God has provided the lamb, just as Abraham said He would.

Hebrews quotes the oath of Genesis 22:16-17, 'I will surely bless you and multiply your descendants,' and explains that God swore by Himself because there was no one greater. The oath and the promise are two unchangeable things that anchor Christian hope.

Solomon built the temple 'on Mount Moriah.' This is the only other mention of Moriah in Scripture and links Abraham's altar to the site where Israel's sacrifices would be offered for centuries, the mountain of the LORD where He provided.

God condemns the burning of children in the Valley of Hinnom as 'something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind.' Genesis 22 must be read in this light: the LORD tested Abraham but never desired Isaac's death, and He stopped the knife.

Moses tells Israel at Sinai that 'God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you.' Testing and the fear of God appear together, just as in Genesis 22:1 and 22:12, where the test ends with 'now I know that you fear God.'

God confirms to Isaac 'the oath that I swore to your father Abraham,' repeating the promise of Genesis 22:17-18 and giving the reason, 'because Abraham listened to My voice.' The oath on Moriah is passed down to the son who lay on the altar.

Peter quotes Genesis 22:18, 'Through your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed,' and says God raised up His Servant and sent Him to bless Israel by turning them from wickedness. The promise sworn on Moriah is fulfilled in the risen Christ.

Jesus says Abraham 'rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad.' Whatever Abraham grasped on Moriah, Jesus presents Himself as the fulfilment Abraham looked forward to, the day when God would provide.

study.oneStory:
Since Genesis 3 the Bible has been asking how sinners can come near to a holy God, and since Genesis 12 how the promised blessing for all nations will come. Genesis 22 brings both questions to a single mountain. The promise is embodied in one son, and God asks for that son as a burnt offering. If Isaac dies, the promise dies. The whole story of redemption seems to stand on the edge of the knife.

The answer is substitution. A ram dies in Isaac's place, and the son lives. This answers what came before. Abel had offered from his flock, Noah had offered burnt offerings after the flood, and Abraham had built altars wherever he went. Now the meaning of sacrifice is made plain: a life given in place of another. It also sets up what comes after. The Passover lamb saves Israel's firstborn in Egypt. Every firstborn son must be redeemed. The whole sacrificial system of Leviticus unfolds the principle of a substitute, and the temple itself is built on Mount Moriah.

Yet all of this remains incomplete. The ram saved one son for a time; the animals of the temple could not take away sin. The question Isaac asked, 'where is the lamb?', echoes through the centuries until John the Baptist points to Jesus. In Jerusalem, the city of Moriah, God does what He stopped Abraham from doing. He gives His own Son. The Son carries the wood, is bound and nailed, and dies, and on the third day He is raised. The oath sworn on Moriah, that all nations would be blessed through Abraham's offspring, is fulfilled as the gospel goes out to the ends of the earth.

The new creation completes the story. John sees 'a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue,' standing 'before the throne and before the Lamb,' Revelation 7:9. They are the descendants promised to Abraham, as many as the stars and the sand, gathered because God provided the Lamb. There is no temple in the city, 'because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. The mountain of the LORD has become the whole new creation, and what was provided there is praised forever.

quiz.q: What was the purpose of God's command to sacrifice Isaac?

options.text: To test and prove Abraham's faith, never intending Isaac actually to die.
options.note: Verse 1 says God tested Abraham, and He stops the sacrifice and provides a ram.

options.text: To bring Abraham's trust to its fullest expression through obedience.
options.note: True and closely related, though it slightly narrows the point that this was a test God controlled from the start.

options.text: Because God delights in human sacrifice like the surrounding nations.
options.note: The opposite is true; God halts the act, and Scripture condemns human sacrifice.

options.text: Because God had changed His mind about the promise through Isaac.
options.note: God renews the promise at the end; He never abandons it.

quiz.q: What did Abraham say when Isaac asked where the lamb was?

options.text: God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering.
options.note: Abraham's words in verse 8 express trust that God will see to the sacrifice.

options.text: That they would find an animal along the way.
options.note: He trusts in provision, but he names God as the provider, not chance.

options.text: That Isaac himself was to be the offering.
options.note: Though this was the command, Abraham's answer points to God's provision instead.

options.text: That there was no need for a lamb at all.
options.note: Abraham fully expects a sacrifice; he trusts God to supply it.

quiz.q: What was provided in Isaac's place?

options.text: A ram caught by its horns in a thicket, offered as a burnt offering.
options.note: Verse 13 records the ram given as a substitute for Isaac.

options.text: A lamb sent down from heaven.
options.note: A substitute is provided, but it is a ram caught in a thicket, not a lamb from the sky.

options.text: One of Abraham's own flock that he had brought.
options.note: The ram was provided by God on the spot, not brought from Abraham's flock.

options.text: Nothing; Isaac was released with no sacrifice made.
options.note: A real sacrifice was made, the ram in Isaac's place.

quiz.q: How does this chapter point forward to Christ?

options.text: A father gives up his only, beloved son, who carries the wood, and God provides the substitute lamb.
options.note: The pattern of beloved son, wood, and provided lamb points to the cross.

options.text: It shows that faithful people will always be spared suffering.
options.note: This misreads the comfort; at the cross the Son was not spared, which is the deeper point.

options.text: It teaches that God tests everyone in exactly this way.
options.note: The test is unique to Abraham; the enduring pattern is the provided substitute, not identical tests.

options.text: It proves that God ultimately requires no sacrifice for sin.
options.note: The chapter centres on a substitute dying, pointing to the sacrifice of Christ.

quiz.q: What does the angel commend in Abraham?

options.text: That he fears God, shown by not withholding his only son.
options.note: Verse 12 names the fear of God, a reverent trust that holds nothing back.

options.text: That he was willing to obey even a hard command.
options.note: His obedience is real, but the text names it specifically as the fear of God.

options.text: That he argued God out of the command.
options.note: Abraham does not argue here; he obeys and trusts God to provide.

options.text: That he loved Isaac more than anything else.
options.note: The commendation is the reverse: he did not put even his beloved son above God.

questions: God asked Abraham for the dearest thing he had. Is there something you are holding so tightly that it has taken God's place in your heart?
Abraham obeyed step by step, trusting God with the outcome he could not see. Where is God calling you to obey before you understand how it will turn out?
Abraham said God Himself will provide, and God did. How have you seen God provide in your own story, and how does that steady you now?
At the cross God did not spare His own Son for you. How does the depth of that gift change the way you face your own costly obedience?
The place was named The LORD Will Provide. What situation do you need to bring to God, trusting Him to see to it in His way and time?

translationNotes.note: The land of Moriah is later associated with the temple mount in Jerusalem, 2 Chronicles 3:1, linking this mountain of sacrifice to the place of Israel's worship.
The name Abraham gives, YHWH Yireh, means The LORD Will See or The LORD Will Provide; the Hebrew verb for see and provide is the same, tying Abraham's trust in verse 8 to the naming here.
